{{short description|On extending a Lie group action on a manifold to an equivariant diffeomorphism}}
In [[differential geometry]], the '''slice theorem''' states:<ref>{{harvnb|Audin|2004|loc=Theorem I.2.1}}</ref> given a [[manifold]] <math>M</math> on which a [[Lie group]] ''<math>G</math>'' [[Lie group action|acts]] as [[diffeomorphism]]s, for any ''<math>x</math>'' in ''<math>M</math>'', the map <math>G/G_x \to M, \, [g] \mapsto g \cdot x</math> extends to an invariant neighborhood of <math>G/G_x</math> (viewed as a zero section)  in <math>G \times_{G_x} T_x M / T_x(G \cdot x)</math> so that it defines an [[equivariant]] diffeomorphism from the neighborhood to its image, which contains the orbit of ''<math>x</math>''.

The important application of the theorem is a proof of the fact that the quotient <math>M/G</math> admits a manifold structure when ''<math>G</math>'' is compact and the action is free.

In [[algebraic geometry]], there is an analog of the slice theorem; it is called [[Luna's slice theorem]].

== Idea of proof when ''G'' is compact ==
Since ''<math>G</math>'' is compact, there exists an invariant metric; i.e., ''<math>G</math>'' acts as [[isometries]]. One then adapts the usual proof of the existence of a tubular neighborhood using this metric.

==See also==
*[[Luna's slice theorem]], an analogous result for [[reductive algebraic group]] actions on [[algebraic variety|algebraic varieties]]
